title: The annual update cycle and what actually changes
description: ICD-10-CM and CPT update on predictable annual cycles with a knowable structure — new codes, deleted codes, and revised guidelines — and knowing that structure in advance turns an update from a surprise into a routine, checkable task.

learningObjectives.text: Describe the predictable structure of the annual ICD-10-CM and CPT update cycle
Distinguish the three kinds of annual change (additions, deletions, guideline revisions) and their different practical implications

contentSections.title: A predictable cycle, not a surprise

contentSections.body: A reviewer who's been coasting on what they learned in this track a year ago approves a proposed code that was valid last year and was deleted, replaced by a more specific pair of codes, effective October 1st. Nothing about this was unpredictable — the update happens on the same date every year, and it was published months in advance.

contentSections.scenario: ICD-10-CM updates annually, with a fixed effective date and a known publication lead time before that date, giving reviewers a predictable window to review what's changing before it takes effect.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many weeks or months of advance notice does the published annual ICD-10-CM update typically give, between publication and its effective date?
contentSections.explanation: ICD-10-CM updates take effect October 1st each year (the start of the federal fiscal year), with the update files typically published by CMS/NCHS around June, giving roughly three to four months of advance notice before the effective date. CPT updates follow a different annual cycle, typically effective January 1st, with codes released by the AMA in the preceding months. Neither cycle is a surprise to anyone checking on a predictable schedule — the actual risk isn't the update happening, it's not having a routine that checks for it.

contentSections.body: The practical structure worth internalizing: every annual update contains three distinct kinds of change, and they have different implications for a reviewer. New codes require learning what's now codeable that wasn't before — often reflecting newly recognized conditions or increased specificity for existing ones. Deleted codes require knowing what's no longer valid, since a pipeline that hasn't been updated might still propose a code that's now invalid, which a reviewer needs to catch even if the AI's pipeline itself lags. Guideline revisions are the subtlest and most consequential — the same code might still exist, but the rule for when to use it, or how to sequence it against other codes, can change without any code itself changing, which means "the code exists" is not the same claim as "the code is still used the same way."
The annual update has three distinct parts — new codes, deleted codes, and guideline revisions — and a code still existing doesn't mean its usage rules haven't changed.

contentSections.title: Why AI pipelines lag, specifically

contentSections.scenario: An AI coding-assist pipeline, six weeks after October 1st, still proposes a code that was deleted and replaced on that date. The vendor's changelog shows the model update addressing the new code set shipped eight weeks after the effective date.
contentSections.question: What's the structural reason an AI pipeline's code-set knowledge tends to lag the actual effective date, rather than updating automatically on the date itself?

options.label: Retraining or updating a model's or ruleset's knowledge of a new code set is itself a development task with its own timeline, which doesn't automatically synchronize with the regulatory effective date — the vendor has to notice, build, test, and ship the update
AI pipelines always update instantly on the effective date, so this shouldn't be possible
This specific pipeline is unusually broken; well-built pipelines don't have this problem at all

contentSections.mechanism: A regulatory effective date and a vendor's engineering release cycle are two independent processes — the code set changes on a fixed calendar date regardless of any vendor's readiness, but incorporating that change into a model or rules engine requires the vendor to notice the update, build and test the change, and ship a release, which realistically takes some number of weeks and varies by vendor. This is a structural, not exceptional, gap — which is exactly why a human reviewer's own independent knowledge of the update cycle is a real safeguard, not a redundant one, during the specific window after an effective date and before a given pipeline catches up.

contentSections.body: This is the direct, practical reason this lesson matters for the job, not just as background knowledge: during the weeks after each annual effective date, a reviewer who knows the update independently is often ahead of the pipeline itself, and that gap is precisely when a reviewer's own knowledge catches errors the pipeline is still making. This is a second, distinct application of the reviewer-not-clerk framing from early in this track — verifying the AI's proposed code against current guidelines, not just against what the AI was trained on.

An AI pipeline's code-set knowledge lags the regulatory effective date by however long the vendor's own update cycle takes — which is exactly the window where a reviewer's independent, current knowledge catches errors the pipeline is still making.

title: Reading official guidelines efficiently
description: The official ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines for Coding and Reporting document is long and not written to be read cover to cover — a targeted reading strategy, checking only the sections relevant to your own review queue's specialty mix, makes annual review realistic on a small time budget.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a targeted reading strategy to the official coding guidelines document rather than reading it linearly
Identify which sections of the guidelines are relevant to a specific reviewer's actual queue composition

contentSections.title: Reading a 100-plus-page document is the wrong plan

contentSections.body: The official ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines for Coding and Reporting document runs well over a hundred pages, covering every specialty and chapter of the code set. A reviewer whose queue is overwhelmingly diabetes- and cardiovascular-documentation-heavy doesn't need to read the obstetrics chapter cover to cover every year — and trying to is exactly the kind of plan that gets abandoned by week two.

contentSections.question: Given a reviewer whose queue composition is known (say, mostly endocrine and cardiovascular documentation, per this lesson's example), what's the more realistic annual reading strategy than reading the full guidelines document linearly?
contentSections.answer: Read the general coding guidelines section (which applies across all specialties, and is comparatively short) in full, then jump directly to the chapter-specific guideline sections that match your own queue's actual composition, skimming or skipping chapters that essentially never appear in your review queue. This mirrors the same targeted-reading discipline as reading a job posting for its actual binding requirements rather than every line with equal weight — spend the limited reading budget where it actually changes what you'd do.
contentSections.hint: Compare this to how the credentials module taught reading a job posting — reading every line with equal weight, or targeting the parts that actually matter to your situation?

contentSections.body: The "what changed" summary published alongside each annual update is the other major time-saver worth using deliberately: CMS and the AMA both publish summary documents specifically listing what's new, deleted, or revised for the year, rather than requiring a reviewer to diff the entire document themselves. Reading the summary first, then only diving into the full guideline text for changes that touch your own queue's specialty mix, turns an unrealistic full-document annual read into a targeted, much shorter task — the same triage principle as reading a job posting's requirement section for what's actually binding, applied here to a much longer document.

Read the general guidelines in full, use the published "what changed" summary as your first pass, and only dive into full guideline text for chapters that actually match your own queue's specialty composition.

contentSections.title: Building this into something repeatable, not a one-time slog

contentSections.question: Put these into the order a sustainable annual guideline-reading routine should follow.
steps: Read the published summary of what's new, deleted, or revised for the year
Identify which changed items fall within your own queue's specialty mix
Read the general coding guidelines section in full (short, applies across specialties)
Read the full guideline text only for the specific chapters containing changes relevant to your queue
contentSections.explanation: The efficient order starts broad and short — general guidelines, which apply everywhere and aren't long — then uses the summary to triage what's actually changed, filters that down to what's relevant to your own queue, and only then spends time in the full guideline text, and only for the specific relevant chapters. Reading the full document cover to cover first, or skipping the summary and hunting through the whole document for changes, both waste the limited time budget this lesson is trying to protect.

contentSections.body: Read general guidelines first, use the annual summary to triage what changed, then spend targeted time only in the chapters that match your own queue — not the whole document, every year, cover to cover.

title: Tracking the pipeline changes at your own employer
description: Code-set updates are external and public; a specific employer's AI pipeline changes (model updates, ruleset tweaks, new confidence thresholds) are internal and often under-communicated — tracking them requires a different, more active habit than checking a public calendar.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish external code-set changes from internal pipeline changes as needing different tracking habits
Design a habit for staying informed about an employer's own pipeline changes given typical under-communication

contentSections.title: Two different kinds of change, two different habits

contentSections.body: The annual code-set update is public, scheduled, and documented months in advance. A vendor's model update that changes the pipeline's confidence-scoring behavior can ship on any Tuesday with a one-line internal changelog entry nobody on the review team reads. These require genuinely different tracking habits, and conflating them is a real risk.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer notices, over about two weeks, that the AI pipeline's confidence scores for a specific category of chart have shifted noticeably higher on average — cases that would previously have landed in the review queue as lower-confidence are now sailing through at high confidence. No announcement was made about a pipeline change.
contentSections.question: What's the appropriate response, given that this is an internal pipeline change rather than a public code-set update?

options.label: Raise it proactively with a supervisor or the pipeline team — internal changes are often under-communicated to reviewers, and noticing a real shift is itself valuable information worth surfacing, not something to wait for an announcement about
Assume it's fine, since if something important changed, someone would have announced it
Treat it the same as an annual code-set update and check the public CMS/AMA calendar for an explanation

feedback.raise: Right. Internal pipeline changes — model updates, threshold tweaks, ruleset adjustments — are, realistically, often under-communicated to the reviewers who actually work downstream of them, for reasons ranging from organizational silos to a vendor update simply not being flagged as reviewer-relevant. A reviewer noticing a real behavioral shift and proactively raising it is exactly the kind of vigilance this whole track has been building, applied to a new context: not catching one wrong chart, but catching a systemic shift.
feedback.assume: Assuming silence means nothing changed is exactly the automation-bias-adjacent mistake this track has warned against in a different form — trusting an absence of information as if it were positive information, which it isn't. Internal changes are structurally likely to go under-communicated, not because anyone is hiding anything, but because the communication path from a vendor's engineering team to a frontline reviewer is often genuinely weak.
feedback.public: The public code-set calendar has no bearing on an internal pipeline or vendor model update — these are separate change categories with separate (and separately unreliable) communication channels, which is exactly the point of this lesson.

contentSections.concept: Internal pipeline changes need an active, self-initiated tracking habit — noticing behavioral shifts and raising them — because the communication channel from vendor/engineering to reviewer is structurally weaker than the public code-set update calendar.

contentSections.body: A public code-set update has a reliable communication channel (an annual calendar); an internal pipeline change usually doesn't — noticing a shift and raising it proactively is the reviewer's own responsibility, not something to wait to be told about.

contentSections.title: Building the actual habit

contentSections.intro: Design a lightweight habit for tracking an employer's internal pipeline changes, given that formal communication about them is often unreliable.

fields.prompt: How often should a reviewer actively check for signs of pipeline change, given this isn't on a predictable public calendar?
options: A brief, regular check-in (e.g. monthly) comparing rough confidence-score patterns or common flag types against what feels familiar, even without a formal report
Daily deep audits of every single chart's confidence score
fields.correctValue: A brief, regular check-in (e.g. monthly) comparing rough confidence-score patterns or common flag types against what feels familiar, even without a formal report
fields.feedback: "Only when something obviously breaks" misses the gradual, hard-to-notice shifts this lesson is specifically about — by the time something obviously breaks, a subtler shift may have been running unnoticed for weeks. Daily deep audits are unsustainable and unnecessary; a brief, regular check-in is the sustainable middle path, matching this track's general pattern-over-perfection approach to self-monitoring.

fields.prompt: Where should a noticed shift actually be raised?
options: Nowhere — reviewers aren't positioned to comment on pipeline behavior
Directly to a supervisor or whoever owns the pipeline relationship, specifically and with an example, not as a vague complaint
Only in an anonymous suggestion box, if one exists
fields.correctValue: Directly to a supervisor or whoever owns the pipeline relationship, specifically and with an example, not as a vague complaint
fields.feedback: Reviewers are, in fact, uniquely positioned to notice pipeline behavioral shifts, since they're the ones actually looking at outputs daily — raising it specifically and directly, with a concrete example, is far more actionable than a vague complaint or no channel at all.

fields.prompt: Should a noticed shift be documented, even informally, before raising it?
options: No, just mention it verbally in passing
Yes — even a brief informal note (what changed, roughly when noticed, a specific example chart) makes the report far more useful and credible than an impression stated from memory
Only if it's already causing a visible problem
fields.correctValue: Yes — even a brief informal note (what changed, roughly when noticed, a specific example chart) makes the report far more useful and credible than an impression stated from memory
fields.feedback: The same evidence-citing discipline from the portfolio module's write-up structure applies here — a specific, documented example is far more useful and credible to whoever receives the report than a vague, undocumented impression, and it costs very little extra time to jot down as it's noticed.

contentSections.synthesis: A sustainable pipeline-tracking habit is a brief, regular (not daily, not only-when-broken) check-in, a specific example documented as it's noticed, and a direct, specific report to whoever owns the pipeline relationship — not silence, not a vague complaint, and not an unsustainable daily audit.

contentSections.body: Track internal pipeline changes with a brief, regular check-in, document specific examples as they're noticed, and raise them directly and specifically — this habit has to be self-initiated, since the formal communication channel usually isn't reliable.

title: Continuing education that's worth the hours
description: Continuing education requirements exist to maintain most coding credentials, but not all CE hours are equally worth spending limited time and money on — a filter based on this module's own priorities (update-cycle relevance, pipeline literacy) helps choose well among a large field of options.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a continuing-education option against specific, stated criteria rather than availability or marketing alone
Prioritize CE hours toward content that directly extends this module's skills

contentSections.title: A large field of options, unevenly worth your hours

contentSections.body: A CPC credential holder needs a set number of continuing-education units (CEUs) every renewal cycle to maintain certification. The catalog of qualifying courses is enormous — webinars, conference sessions, self-paced modules — and most of it isn't equally relevant to an AI-oversight coding review role specifically.

contentSections.scenario: Four CE options, each qualifying for the same number of CEUs: (1) "Annual ICD-10-CM Update Deep Dive," covering the current year's specific code and guideline changes. (2) "Fundamentals of Medical Terminology," an introductory-level refresher course. (3) "AI and Automation in Clinical Documentation: What Reviewers Need to Know," covering how AI-assisted coding pipelines actually work and common failure patterns. (4) "Advanced Billing for Ambulatory Surgical Centers," a specialty deep-dive unrelated to the reviewer's actual queue.
contentSections.question: Given this module's priorities (staying current on updates and pipeline literacy) and a limited annual CE hour budget, which options are the strongest use of that budget? Select all that apply.

items.label: Annual ICD-10-CM Update Deep Dive
Fundamentals of Medical Terminology (introductory refresher)
AI and Automation in Clinical Documentation: What Reviewers Need to Know
Advanced Billing for Ambulatory Surgical Centers (unrelated specialty)

explanation.update: Directly extends lesson one and two's content — this is exactly the kind of CE hour that keeps a reviewer current on the specific thing that changes every year and needs active tracking.
explanation.terminology: An introductory refresher is real content, but for someone who's completed this track, it's very likely covering ground already well established — a CEU spent here isn't a bad use in an absolute sense, just a lower-value one relative to the alternatives, unless there's a specific personal knowledge gap it addresses.
explanation.ai: Directly extends this module's pipeline-literacy content — understanding how AI-assisted coding actually works and its common failure patterns is squarely relevant to the specific role this whole track prepares for, more than most general CE catalog offerings.
explanation.billing: Real, useful content for someone whose queue actually includes ambulatory surgical center billing — but for a reviewer whose queue doesn't touch that specialty, it's CE time spent on content with no near-term application, which is the specific pattern this lesson is arguing against defaulting into.

contentSections.synthesis: Not all CEUs are equal in relevance even when they're equal in credit — prioritizing CE hours toward update-cycle content and pipeline literacy specifically, rather than whatever's available or unrelated-but-interesting, keeps a limited annual hour budget pointed at what actually extends this role's specific skill set.

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument for narrowness for its own sake — a reviewer whose queue genuinely does include ambulatory surgical center documentation should absolutely prioritize that specialty's CE content; the filter is "relevant to my actual queue and role," not "relevant to this module's specific two examples." The general principle is choosing CE hours the same deliberate way lesson four of the credentials module taught choosing a certification: against a specific, stated need, not against whatever's on the top of a catalog page or has the most appealing title.

Filter continuing-education choices against your own actual queue and role, prioritizing update-cycle and pipeline-literacy content specifically — not whichever course has the most appealing title or happens to be first in a catalog.

contentSections.title: A small, sustainable annual CE routine

contentSections.question: If your renewal deadline is eight months away and you haven't started any CE hours yet, what's the better move: one long weekend course covering the full requirement, or spreading it out starting now?
contentSections.answer: Spread it out starting now — the same spaced-versus-concentrated logic from the credentials module's study-timeline lesson applies to CE hours too: many small sessions are far more resilient to a bad month than a single large block, and starting immediately, even at a slow pace, removes the deadline-panic version of CE entirely.
contentSections.hint: Compare this to the credentials module's argument against a three-weekend cram plan for exam study.

contentSections.body: The same energy-aware pacing principle from the credentials module's study-timeline lesson applies directly to CE hours: spreading a year's required CEUs across small, regular sessions (one short session a month, roughly) is more sustainable than a single marathon push near a renewal deadline, and it naturally aligns well with this module's own update cycle — scheduling the annual-update-focused CE session for shortly after each October 1st effective date, when the year's actual changes are freshest and most directly checkable against real review work, makes the CE hour immediately useful rather than abstract.

Spread CE hours across small, regular sessions rather than a deadline-driven push, and time the update-focused session to land shortly after the annual effective date, when it's most immediately useful.

title: A yearly refresh routine you'll actually do
description: This module's separate pieces — update tracking, guideline reading, pipeline vigilance, CE selection — combine into a single small yearly routine, timed around the October 1st effective date, sized to actually get done rather than sized to look thorough on paper.

learningObjectives.text: Assemble this module's individual skills into a single, realistic, recurring yearly routine
Size a recurring professional-maintenance routine to what will actually get done, not to an idealized maximum

contentSections.title: A routine sized to actually happen

contentSections.body: A routine that reads impressively on paper — read the full guidelines document, review every pipeline changelog, complete a full CE course, all within the first week of October — is exactly the kind of ambitious plan that gets attempted once, exhausts the person attempting it, and never happens again. A smaller routine that actually recurs every year beats a comprehensive one that runs once.

contentSections.question: Given everything this module has covered, what's the single smallest version of an annual refresh routine that would still meaningfully cover the core risk (missing a real update)?
contentSections.answer: Something like: read the published "what changed" summary (lesson two) within a few weeks of the October 1st effective date, check it against your own queue's specialty mix, and spend CE time only on the specific changes that actually apply to you — skipping the full guideline document entirely unless a specific change genuinely warrants it. This alone catches the highest-risk gap (a genuinely relevant deleted or revised code you didn't know about) without requiring the full, unsustainable version of the routine.
contentSections.hint: Which single piece of this module's content, done alone, would catch the highest-risk gap — a real, queue-relevant change you didn't know about — with the least total time?

contentSections.body: This is the same principle the credentials module applied to a bad-day study session and the earlier module applied to a bad-week job search: define the smallest version that still does the actual job, explicitly, in advance — not as a fallback to feel guilty about using, but as the actual default plan. A yearly refresh routine sized to the smallest-version-that-still-works is far more likely to actually happen every single year, for years, than an ambitious full version that looks better on paper but only survives one cycle before being abandoned.
Size the yearly routine to its smallest version that still catches the real risk — a routine that actually happens every year beats a comprehensive one that only happens once.

contentSections.title: Putting a date on it

contentSections.question: Suppose the smallest-version routine from earlier in this lesson gets skipped one year entirely, for a genuinely bad year. What's the right response the following year?
contentSections.answer: Resume the routine as normal the next cycle rather than trying to retroactively make up the missed year all at once — the same principle as a skipped study week in the credentials module: a missed cycle doesn't need to be recovered in a lump, it needs the routine to simply continue on schedule going forward.
contentSections.hint: What did the credentials module say about a missed study week — try to make it up all at once, or just resume the normal schedule?

contentSections.body: The last practical piece is attaching the routine to a fixed, recurring calendar date rather than leaving it as a vague intention — something like "the second week of October, every year" (a couple weeks after the effective date, once the update summary and any early pipeline-lag issues are visible) turns "I should stay current" into a specific, schedulable, recurring task the same way a checkpoint or a study session became a specific scheduled thing earlier in this track, rather than a value someone holds abstractly and never quite gets to. This is, in miniature, the same shift this entire phase has been arguing for throughout — from good intentions to specific, sized, dated plans.
Attach the yearly refresh routine to a specific recurring calendar date, not a vague ongoing intention — a dated, sized, recurring task is what actually happens; an abstract value rarely does.

If a drill needed the hint to distinguish a public code-set change from an internal pipeline change, that's the distinction to review once more before the lab.

title: Run one annual update review
description: Run a real (or realistic) annual update review end to end — reading a real or constructed update summary, identifying what's queue-relevant, and naming what changes as a result of the review.

learningObjectives.text: Execute a complete, targeted annual update review producing a specific findings list
Translate update findings into concrete changes to personal review practice

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is lesson one through three's content, actually run once, on a real or realistic update cycle — the annual review this module has been building toward, done for real rather than described in the abstract.

contentSections.title: Run one annual update review
contentSections.brief: Using a real recent ICD-10-CM/CPT annual update summary (if accessible) or a constructed, realistic set of 8-10 changes (new codes, deleted codes, guideline revisions) representative of a real annual cycle, run a full targeted review against a stated queue specialty mix, and produce a findings document naming what changed, what's relevant, and what you'd do differently.
contentSections.deliverable: An update-review document: the queue specialty mix you're reviewing against, the full list of changes considered, which ones are relevant to that queue (with a one-line reason each), and — for each relevant change — one concrete thing you'd do differently in review practice as a result.

stages.title: Gather the update and state your queue mix
stages.instructions: Find a real recent annual update summary, or construct 8-10 realistic changes (mix of new codes, deleted codes, and guideline revisions) representative of a real cycle. State the specialty mix of the queue you're reviewing against (real or constructed — e.g. "mostly endocrine and cardiovascular documentation").
stages.checkpoint: 8-10 changes exist, spanning all three change types, and a specific queue specialty mix is named.

stages.title: Triage for relevance
stages.instructions: For each change, decide whether it's relevant to the stated queue mix, with a one-line reason either way — following lesson two's targeted-reading approach rather than treating every change as equally worth deep attention.
stages.checkpoint: Every change has a relevance decision and a one-line reason, and the reasons connect specifically to the stated queue mix, not a generic justification.

stages.title: Translate relevant changes into practice changes
stages.instructions: For each change marked relevant, write one concrete thing that changes in your actual review practice as a result — what you'd now check for, what you'd flag differently, or what you'd expect the AI pipeline to still be getting wrong during its own lag window (per lesson one).
stages.checkpoint: Every relevant change has a specific, concrete practice change attached — not a restatement of the update itself, but an actual behavior change.

rubric.criterion: The change set spans all three types (new, deleted, guideline revision)
rubric.meets: At least one item of each of the three types appears in the 8-10 changes considered.

rubric.criterion: Relevance triage is specific to the stated queue mix, not generic
rubric.meets: Each relevance reason references the actual named specialty mix, not a general statement like "this seems important."

rubric.criterion: Each relevant change produces a concrete practice change
rubric.meets: The practice change describes a specific, checkable behavior difference, not a restatement of the update.

rubric.criterion: At least one item explicitly accounts for the AI pipeline's likely update lag
rubric.meets: At least one practice change names something to watch for specifically because the pipeline may not have caught up yet, per lesson one.

rubric.criterion: The whole document is usable as a real reference, not just a completed exercise
rubric.meets: A reviewer could actually use this document's findings in their next real review session without needing to redo the analysis.

title: Checkpoint — Staying Current in Clinical Coding
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous module (Accommodation and Disclosure), two from three-or-more modules back (Interviews and Coding Tests).

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and earlier modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Staying Current in Clinical Coding

questions.from: This module — Staying Current in Clinical Coding
questions.prompt: What are the three distinct kinds of change in an annual code-set update?

options.label: New codes, deleted codes, and guideline revisions
Only new codes — deletions and guideline changes don't happen annually
Federal, state, and private-payer changes

questions.explanation: A code still existing doesn't mean its usage rules haven't changed — guideline revisions can occur without any code itself changing.

questions.from: This module — Staying Current in Clinical Coding
questions.prompt: Why does an AI pipeline's code-set knowledge typically lag the regulatory effective date?

options.label: Incorporating the update into a model or ruleset is a separate engineering task with its own timeline, independent of the regulatory date
AI pipelines update automatically and instantly on the effective date
Only poorly built pipelines have this problem

questions.explanation: The regulatory effective date and a vendor's release cycle are independent processes — this is a structural gap, not an exceptional failure.

questions.from: This module — Staying Current in Clinical Coding
questions.prompt: What's the recommended first step in a targeted annual guideline-reading strategy?

options.label: Read the published summary of what's new, deleted, or revised for the year
Read the entire guidelines document cover to cover, every year
Skip the guidelines entirely and rely on the AI pipeline to have caught everything

questions.explanation: The published summary lets a reviewer triage what's changed before spending time in the full document, targeting only chapters relevant to their own queue.

questions.from: This module — Staying Current in Clinical Coding
questions.prompt: Why is silence about a pipeline change not a safe assumption that nothing changed?

options.label: Internal pipeline changes are structurally likely to be under-communicated to reviewers, unlike the public code-set update calendar
Pipeline changes are always announced clearly and promptly
Pipeline changes never actually affect confidence scores or flag rates

questions.explanation: The communication path from vendor/engineering to a frontline reviewer is often genuinely weak, which is why noticing and proactively raising a shift is the reviewer's own responsibility.

questions.from: Previous module — Accommodation and Disclosure
questions.prompt: What's generally sufficient to open an accommodation conversation, without naming a specific diagnosis?

options.label: Functional-need language describing what's needed to perform the job's essential functions
A formal diagnosis disclosed directly to the hiring manager
Nothing — a diagnosis is always required first

questions.explanation: Functional-need language is generally sufficient to open the conversation; formal documentation, if needed, goes through a separate process.

questions.from: Previous module — Accommodation and Disclosure
questions.prompt: Which accommodations are most specifically relevant to AI-oversight coding review, versus a generic workplace accommodation?

options.label: Volume distribution flexibility, flexible micro-breaks, and shorter review batches
An ergonomic keyboard and a standing desk
Scent-free office policies

questions.explanation: This role's actual demands are pacing and sustained attention, not physical posture, so the most relevant accommodations target those directly.

questions.from: Previous module — Accommodation and Disclosure
questions.prompt: Why does an apologetic, pre-conceding accommodation request tend to invite more negotiation?

options.label: It frames the request as an imposition before the employer responds, signaling it's up for debate rather than a normal operational matter
Employers always prefer more detailed, apologetic requests
Framing makes no real difference to outcomes

questions.explanation: A plainly stated request treats the ask as normal and operational; an apologetic one invites exactly the negotiation-about-worthiness dynamic it's trying to avoid.

questions.from: Previous module — Accommodation and Disclosure
questions.prompt: What distinguishes ordinary friction from a real pattern worth reading as a leave signal?

options.label: A single instance corrected in good faith is ordinary; a repeated pattern of re-justification or quiet punishment is real diagnostic information
Any friction at all means the employer is a bad fit
Friction should never be read as meaningful

questions.explanation: Occasional forgetting with genuine correction is healthy; repeated re-litigation or unexplained reduced opportunity is a real, actionable pattern.

questions.from: Three modules back — Interviews and Coding Tests
questions.prompt: A coding-review test rubric weights flagging genuine uncertainty as equal to correctly identifying an error. What does this reveal?

options.label: The test is measuring reasoning process — evidence-checking and honest uncertainty — not just raw speed or a perfect score
Uncertainty flags are a scoring loophole unrelated to real skill
The fastest finisher is still the intended winner

questions.explanation: A rubric built by someone who's run a real review pipeline tends to reward the reasoning process that prevents confident-wrongness.

questions.from: Three modules back — Interviews and Coding Tests
questions.prompt: Which employer answer to a volume-target question is the strongest positive signal?

options.label: A specific number, plus explicit flexibility in how the total is distributed across the week
"We don't track it, just do your best"
A hard daily number tracked hourly with no exceptions

questions.explanation: A specific number combined with real distribution flexibility best supports sustainable, variable-capacity pacing.
